questions.stem:
Given that $n$ is an integer, use algebra, to prove by contradiction, that if $n^3$ is even then $n$ is even.
(4)

parts.text:
Given that $n$ is an integer, use algebra, to prove by contradiction, that if $n^3$ is even then $n$ is even.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: For setting up the contradiction, e.g. Assume that there exists a number $m$ such that when $m^3$ is even, $m$ is odd. Condone a contra-positive statement here.
M1: Attempts to cube an odd number. Accept an attempt at $(2p+1)^3$, $(2p-1)^3$.
A1: $(2p+1)^3=8p^3+12p^2+6p+1$ or simplified equivalent such as $2\times(4p^3+6p^2+3p)+1$.
A1: For a fully correct proof. Requires correct calculations with reason and conclusion, e.g. "hence we have a contradiction, so if $n^3$ is even, then $n$ is even."
Official notes (completeness pass):
- "Assume that there exists a number $m$ such that when $m^3$ is even, $m$ is not even" As a minimum accept "assume if $m^3$ is even then $m$ is odd." Condone the other way around " assume if $n$ is odd then $n^3$ is even"
- M1: Look for $(2p+1)^3=...p^3.....$
- A1: For $(2p-1)^3=8p^3-12p^2+6p-1$ or equivalent such as $2\times(4p^3-6p^2+3p-1)+1$
- E.g. 1 Correct calculations $(2p+1)^3=8p^3+12p^2+6p+1=$ Reason (even +1) = odd Conclusion "hence we have a contradiction, so if $n^3$ is even, then $n$ is even." E.g. 2 Correct calculations $(2p+1)^3=8p^3+12p^2+6p+1$ Reason $=2\times(4p^3+6p^2+3p)+1$ = odd Conclusion "this is contradiction, so proven." E.g. 3 Correct calculations $(2p-1)^3=8p^3-12p^2+6p-1$ Reason = $8p^3-12p^2+6p$ is even so $8p^3-12p^2+6p-1$ is odd Conclusion: So if $n^3$ is even then $n$ must be even
- Note that B0 M1 A1 A1 is possible

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Use the binomial expansion to expand
$(4-5x)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \quad |x|<\frac{4}{5}$
in ascending powers of $x$, up to and including the term in $x^2$ giving each coefficient as a fully simplified fraction.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: For taking out a factor of $4^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ or $\frac{1}{2}$.
M1: For the form of the binomial expansion $(1+ax)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ where $a\neq 1$ or $-5$. Allow a slip on the sign.
A1: Any (unsimplified) but correct form of the binomial expansion for $\left(1-\frac{5x}{4}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$.
A1: cao $\frac{1}{2}+\frac{5}{16}x+\frac{75}{256}x^2+...$ This must be simplified.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1: For a direct expansion look for $4^{-\frac{1}{2}}+....$ or equivalent.
- M1: To score M1 it is sufficient to see either term two or term three. So allow for either $\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)(\pm ax)$ or $\frac{\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\times\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)}{2}(\pm ax)^2$ In the alternative version look for $\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)4^{-\frac{3}{2}}(-5x)$ or $\frac{-\frac{1}{2}\times-\frac{3}{2}}{2}4^{-\frac{5}{2}}(-5x)^2$ condoning sign slips
- A1: Ignore the factor preceding the bracket for this mark Score for $1+\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\times\left(-\frac{5x}{4}\right)+\frac{\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\times\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)}{2!}\times\left(-\frac{5x}{4}\right)^2$ o.e. In the alternative version look for $(4-5x)^{-\frac{1}{2}}=4^{-\frac{1}{2}}+\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)4^{-\frac{3}{2}}(-5x)+\frac{-\frac{1}{2}\times-\frac{3}{2}}{2}4^{-\frac{5}{2}}(-5x)^2$
- Alt (a): $4^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ or $\frac{1}{4^{\frac{1}{2}}}$ B1; $(4-5x)^{-\frac{1}{2}}=4^{-\frac{1}{2}}+\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)4^{-\frac{3}{2}}(-5x)+\frac{-\frac{1}{2}\times-\frac{3}{2}}{2}4^{-\frac{5}{2}}(-5x)^2$ M1A1; $=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{5}{16}x+\frac{75}{256}x^2+...$ A1

questions.stem:
Figure 2 shows a sketch of part of the curve with parametric equations
$x=2t^2-6t, \quad y=t^3-4t, \quad t \in \mathbb{R}$
The curve cuts the $x$-axis at the origin and at the points $A$ and $B$, as shown in Figure 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the coordinates of $A$ and show that $B$ has coordinates $(20, 0)$.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Sets $t^3-4t=0 \Rightarrow t=...$ to reach $t=2$ or $-2$
A1: Substitutes $t=2 \Rightarrow x=2\times4-6\times2=-4$ and states coordinates of $A=(-4,0)$
B1*: Show that the coordinates of $B=(20,0)$. This is a show that and there must be some evidence for the "20", not just sight of $t=-2$.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- A1: Accept $t=2\Rightarrow A=(-4,0)$ provided the M1 has been awarded
- B1*: Possible ways of this are 1) Solves $t^3-4t=0\Rightarrow t=-2$ and substitutes into $2t^2-6t\Rightarrow x=20\Rightarrow B=(20,0)$. Look for $2\times(-2)^2-6\times(-2)\Rightarrow x=20$ or $8+12\Rightarrow x=20$
- 2) Alternatively sets $2t^2-6t=20\Rightarrow t=-2$ and substitutes into $y=t^3-4t\to y=0\Rightarrow B=(20,0)$ This is a show that and there must be some evidence for the "0", not just sight of $t=-2$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Show that the equation of the tangent to the curve at $B$ is
$7y+4x-80=0$
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Attempts to differentiate $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ and calculates $\frac{dy}{dx}$ by using $\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}$
A1: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3t^2-4}{4t-6}$
M1: Sub 'their' $t=-2$ into their $\frac{dy}{dx}$ to find the gradient of the tangent at $B$.
M1: Uses $(20,0)$ and their $\frac{dy}{dx}$ to find an equation of the tangent. If they use $y=mx+c$ they need to proceed as far as $c=...$
A1*: Achieves given answer. cso $\Rightarrow 7y+4x-80=0$ The $=0$ must be seen. isw after sight of this.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The tangent to the curve at $B$ cuts the curve again at the point $P$.
(c) Find, using algebra, the $x$ coordinate of $P$.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Attempts to substitute $x=2t^2-6t$, $y=t^3-4t$ into $7y+4x-80=0$
A1: Correct simplified equation in $t$: $7t^3+8t^2-52t-80=0$
dM1: Uses a correct method to find $x$
A1: cso $x=-\frac{40}{49}$. Do not accept decimals here.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- The demand here is to use algebra which is satisfied by the setting up of the cubic equation.
- A1: The $=0$ may be implied by further work
- dM1: Using a calculator this can be scored for finding a value of $t\neq-2$ and substituting this in $x$ ($t$). You may have to check this on a calculator if their equation is incorrect. An accuracy of 2 sf is required for non exact solutions. Note that the equation may be in different forms under this method so $7t^3+8t^2-52t=80\Rightarrow t=\frac{20}{7}$ is fine Note: $7(t^3-4t)+4(2t^2-6t)-80=0\Rightarrow t=\frac{20}{7}\Rightarrow x=-\frac{40}{49}$ would score M1 A0 dM1 A0
- dM1: Via factorisation look for factors where the ends work, E.g. "$7t^3+8t^2-52t-80$"$=(Pt+a)(Qt+b)(Rt+c)$ with $PQR=$"7" and $abc=$"$\pm80$" followed by substitution of a value of $t\neq-2$ in $x$ (t)
- A1: remember to isw following a correct answer. Ignore any references to the $y$ coordinate. Penalise extra solutions, incorrect factorisation etc on this mark.

questions.stem:
Bacteria are growing on the surface of a dish in a laboratory.
The area of the dish, $A\,\mathrm{cm}^2$, covered by the bacteria, $t$ days after the bacteria start to grow, is modelled by the differential equation
$\frac{dA}{dt}=\frac{A^{\frac{3}{2}}}{5t^2} \quad t>0$
Given that $A=2.25$ when $t=3$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) show that
$A=\left(\frac{pt}{qt+r}\right)^2$
where $p$, $q$ and $r$ are integers to be found.
(7)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Attempts to separate the variables either $\int \frac{dA}{A^{3/2}}=\int ... \frac{dt}{t^2}$ oe
M1: Integrates one side correctly. Look for $pA^{-1/2}$ or $qt^{-1}$
dM1: Integrates both sides correctly. Look for $pA^{-1/2}$ and $qt^{-1}$
A1: Correct intermediate stage (without $+c$): $-2A^{-1/2}=-\frac{1}{5}t^{-1}(+c)$ or equivalent
M1: Must have a "$+c$" now. It is for using $t=3$, $A=2.25 \Rightarrow c=...$
M1: It is for proceeding to $A=\left(\frac{pt}{qt+r}\right)^2$ from an equation of the form $\frac{p}{\sqrt{A}}=\frac{q}{t}+r$ with correct operations.
A1: $A=\left(\frac{30t}{19t+3}\right)^2$ cso.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: oe such as $\int...\frac{dA}{A^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\int\frac{dt}{t^2}$ Condone without the integral signs but the $A^{\frac{3}{2}}$, $dA$, $t^2$ and $dt$ must be in the correct positions. Don't be too concerned on the position of the "5"
- A1: Either $-2A^{-\frac{1}{2}}=-\frac{1}{5}t^{-1}(+c)$ or $-10A^{-\frac{1}{2}}=-t^{-1}(+c)$ or equivalent such as $-\frac{A^{-0.5}}{0.5}=-\frac{1}{5}t^{-1}(+c)$
- M1: There must be some evidence for this award which may be implied by their value for c if no working is seen. One index must have started out correct This may be awarded after an incorrect change of subject has occurred.
- M1: Candidates do not need to have found a value for $r$ (their constant) to score this mark The attempt must involve • using a common factor on the rhs of $\frac{p}{\sqrt{A}}=\frac{q}{t}+r$ • "inverting" both sides not each term • an attempt to square both sides and not each term to reach $A=...$
- A1: This mark can be awarded independent of the first M1 Be aware that $A=\left(\frac{300t}{190t+30}\right)^2$ is also correct

parts.label: b
parts.text:
According to the model, there is a limit to the area that will be covered by the bacteria.
(b) Find the value of this limit.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: As $t\to\infty$, $A\to\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^2$. The form of part (a) must be $A=\left(\frac{at}{bt+c}\right)^2$ where $a,b,c$ are all positive.
A1: $\frac{900}{361}$ or awrt $2.49\,\mathrm{cm}^2$ following correct work.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: The reason for this is that if we had "$bt-c$", the area would be infinite at $t=\frac{c}{b}$ and a limit would not exist
- Condone for both marks $A<\frac{900}{361}$ following correct work.
